en: Cūḷaniddesa:
Exposition of the Pārāyaṇa Chapter;
Exposition of the Questions.
13. The Exposition of the Questions of the Young Man Udaya "Seated,
meditating, free from passion," (said the Venerable Udaya).
One who has done what was to be done, who is free from taints,
who has gone beyond all phenomena—
come to me with a question.
"Tell me of the liberation through final knowledge,
the breaking asunder of ignorance,
for the meditator who sits free from passion."
The Blessed One is a meditator who meditates.
He meditates with the first jhāna, he meditates with the second jhāna, he meditates with the third jhāna, he meditates with the fourth jhāna,
and he meditates with the jhāna accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, as well as with the jhāna without applied thought and with only sustained thought.
One who meditates by means of jhāna without applied thought and sustained thought; one who meditates by means of jhāna accompanied by rapture; one who meditates by means of jhāna free from rapture;
one who meditates by means of jhāna accompanied by pleasure; one who meditates by means of jhāna accompanied by equanimity;
one who meditates by means of jhāna that is empty; one who meditates by means of jhāna that is signless; and one who meditates by means of jhāna that is desireless.
One who meditates by means of both mundane jhāna and supramundane jhāna, delighting in jhāna, devoted to unity, and regarding his own goal as weighty—such a one is called a “meditator” (jhāyin).
“Dust-free”: passion is dust, hatred is dust, delusion is dust, anger is dust, resentment is dust … [and so on] … all unwholesome volitional formations are dust.
Those stains have been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One; they are cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
Therefore, the Buddha is free from stain, stainless, dustless, one who has gone beyond stain, one who has relinquished stain, one who is dissociated from stain, and one who has transcended all stain.
Passion is a stain, but it is not called "dust."
"Passion" is a designation for "dust.
Having utterly abandoned this dust, the one with vision is therefore called the Victor, the One Free from Dust.
"Defilement is not called 'dust,' nor is it called 'dirt';
this is a designation for defilement, namely, 'dust.
Having utterly abandoned this dust, the one with vision—"
Therefore, the Conqueror is called "one free from dust.
Delusion is the dust, and it is not called the particle of earth;
"dust" is a designation for delusion.
Having utterly abandoned this dust, the Visionary is therefore called the Victor, free from dust. —[The verse on] freedom from dust... [etc.]...
"Seated"—the Blessed One was seated at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya;
thus, "seated.
Seated on the side of the mountain.
The disciples, possessors of the threefold knowledge who have abandoned death, attend upon the Sage who has gone beyond suffering.
In this way, too, the Blessed One was seated.

Alternatively, because all his feverish restlessness had subsided, the Blessed One was seated—one who has completed the rains retreat, one who has fulfilled the practice, ... [as above] ... for whom there is no further becoming in the cycle of birth and death.
In this way, too, the Blessed One was seated.
"I meditated upon the one seated, free from passion.
Thus spoke the Venerable Udayī.
"Thus" (*iccā*) refers to the grammatical connection of words (*padasandhi*)... [and so on].
"Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment...
"Udaya" is the name of that brahmin... "Abhilāpa"—thus, "the venerable Udaya."

"Having done what was to be done and being free from taints": for the Buddha, the Blessed One, what is to be done and what is not to be done, what is to be performed and what is not to be performed, has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is of a nature not to arise again in the future.
Therefore, the Buddha has "done what was to be done.
And he for whom there is no wavering...
For a bhikkhu whose stream is cut,
who has abandoned what is to be done and what is not to be done, no fever exists.
"Having done what was to be done, free from taints.
Taints (āsava) are the four taints:
the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance.
Those taints have been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One; they are cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
Therefore, the Buddha is "taintless"—one who has done what was to be done and is free from taints.

“‘One who has gone beyond all phenomena,’ said the Blessed One: he has gone beyond all phenomena through direct knowledge, through full understanding, through abandoning, through development, through realization, and through attainment.
He has gone beyond all phenomena through direct knowledge; he has gone beyond all suffering through full understanding; he has gone beyond all defilements through abandoning;
he has gone beyond the four paths through development; he has gone beyond cessation through realization; and he has gone beyond all attainments through attainment.”
Thus he has attained mastery and reached perfection in noble virtue;
he has attained mastery and reached perfection in noble concentration;
he has attained mastery and reached perfection in noble wisdom.
He has attained mastery, he has reached perfection in noble liberation.

He has gone to the further shore, reached the further shore; he has gone to the end, reached the end; he has gone to the limit, reached the limit; he has gone to the boundary, reached the boundary; he has gone to the cessation, reached the cessation;
he has gone to the refuge, reached the refuge; he has gone to the shelter, reached the shelter; he has gone to the protection, reached the protection.
He has reached fearlessness, attained fearlessness; he has reached the deathless, attained the deathless; he has reached the immortal, attained the immortal; he has reached Nibbāna, attained Nibbāna.
Having lived the life and practiced the conduct... [as before] ...there is no further becoming for him in the saṃsāra of birth and death—he is one who has gone beyond all phenomena.

"There is coming for the sake of a question; I have come seeking a question; I have come desiring to ask a question; I have come desiring to hear a question"—thus there is "coming for the sake of a question.

Alternatively, there is the coming, the approaching, the drawing near, the arrival, and the attendance of those who seek a question, who desire to ask a question, and who desire to hear a question—thus too there is "coming for the sake of a question."

Alternatively, there is a tradition regarding the question for you: you are capable, you are competent, and you are able to explain and answer what has been asked by me; you can bear this burden. Thus, too, there is a tradition regarding the question.
"Speak of the liberation through final knowledge" (*aññāvimokkha*): liberation through final knowledge refers to the liberation of arahantship.
"Speak of the liberation of arahantship"—explain it, teach it, describe it, establish it, reveal it, analyze it, make it plain, and clarify it.
"Declare the liberation through final knowledge;

the breaking up of ignorance. The "breaking up of ignorance" means the breaking up, the dispersal, the abandoning, the subsiding, the relinquishing, the allaying, the deathless Nibbāna—this is the breaking up of ignorance.
Therefore that brahmin said:
“To the one sitting in meditation, free from passion,” (thus spoke the Venerable Udaya).
One who has done what was to be done, who is free from taints,
who has gone beyond all phenomena—
I have come to you with a question.
"Tell me of the liberation through final knowledge, the breaking apart of ignorance. [The Blessed One replied:
"The abandoning of sensual desires..."
The Blessed One has arisen,
having dispelled both kinds of mental distress and the removal of sloth.
The warding off of remorse;
the abandoning of sensual desire.

"Sensual desire" (chanda) refers to that which is sensual desire for sense-pleasures, sensual lust, sensual delight, sensual craving, sensual affection, sensual thirst, sensual fever, sensual infatuation, sensual clinging, the flood of sensual pleasure, the yoke of sensual pleasure, the clinging to sensual pleasure, and the hindrance of sensual desire.
"The abandoning of sensual desire" means: the abandoning, the subsiding, the relinquishing, the tranquilization, the deathless Nibbāna of sensual desires—this is "the abandoning of sensual desires.
"The Blessed One is the arising," he said.
The Blessed One addresses that brahmin by name, saying, "Udayī.
"Blessed One" (bhagavā) is a designation for veneration... [as before] ...it is a descriptive term based on realization, namely: "Blessed One"—thus says the Blessed One.
"Both forms of mental distress (*domanassa*).

Mental distress refers to that which is mentally disagreeable, mentally painful, born of mental contact, disagreeable and painful feeling, and the feeling born of mental contact that is disagreeable and painful.
"Both forms of mental distress" means the abandoning, the subsiding, the relinquishing, and the calming of both sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and mental distress—the deathless *nibbāna*.
And the dispelling of sloth: "sloth" (thinam) refers to that state of the mind which is unwholesome,
unwieldy, sluggishness, lingering, being sluggish, the state of being sluggish, sloth, the act of slothing, and the state of having slothed the mind.
They dispel: the dispelling of dullness is its abandoning, its subsiding, its relinquishing, its calming, the deathless, Nibbāna—this is the dispelling of dullness.
The warding off of remorse.
“Remorse” means: remorse regarding the hands is remorse; remorse regarding the feet is remorse; remorse regarding both hands and feet is remorse.

It is the perception of what is allowable as unallowable, and the perception of what is unallowable as allowable … [and so on] … the perception of what is blameless as blameworthy, and the perception of what is blameworthy as blameless.
That which is such remorse, the state of being remorseful, the condition of being remorseful, mental regret, and mental scrupulousness—this is called remorse.
Furthermore, remorse, mental regret, and mental scrupulousness arise for two reasons: on account of what has been done and on account of what has not been done.
How does remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish arise through what has been done and what has not been done?
“I have committed a bodily misconduct; I have failed to perform a bodily good deed”—thus arises remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish.
“I have committed a verbal misconduct; I have failed to perform a verbal good deed”—thus [arises remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish]. …pe…
“I have committed misconduct of the mind; I have not practiced good conduct of the mind” ...
“I have committed the taking of life; I have not practiced abstention from the taking of life” ...
“I have committed taking what is not given; I have not practiced abstention from taking what is not given” ... [and so on].
“I have committed sexual misconduct; I have not practiced abstention from sexual misconduct,” …pe… “I have spoken falsehood;
I have not practiced abstention from falsehood,” …pe… “I have spoken malicious speech;
I have not practiced abstention from malicious speech,” …pe…
“I have committed harsh speech; I have failed to abstain from harsh speech” …pe… “I have engaged in idle chatter;
I have failed to abstain from idle chatter” …pe… “I have harbored covetousness;
I have failed to practice non-covetousness” …pe…
“Malice has been done by me; non-malice has not been done by me” ...
[and so on] ... “Wrong view has been adopted by me; right view has not been adopted by me”—thus there arises remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish.
In this way, remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish arise from what has been done and what has not been done.
Alternatively, there arises remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish [thinking]: "I was one who failed to fulfill my duties regarding the moral precepts";
"I was one who did not guard the doors of the sense faculties"; ...
"I was one who lacked moderation in eating"; ...
“I am not devoted to wakefulness,” … “I am not endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension,” … “The four foundations of mindfulness have not been developed by me;
the four right strivings, the four bases for psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path [have not been developed by me].”

“Suffering has not been fully understood by me; its origin has not been abandoned by me; the path has not been cultivated by me; cessation has not been realized by me”—thus arises remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish.

The warding off of remorse means: the obstruction, hindrance, abandoning, pacification, complete pacification, relinquishment, subsiding, and the deathless Nibbāna of remorses—this is the warding off of remorses.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“The abandoning of sensual desires,” [the Blessed One said].
The dispelling of both types of dejection,
the removal of sloth,
and the prevention of remorse.
I declare that the liberation through final knowledge is purified by equanimity and mindfulness, preceded by reflection on the nature of phenomena.
The breaking up of ignorance.
"Purified by equanimity and mindfulness":
as for "equanimity," it is that equanimity, the act of equanimizing, the thorough equanimizing, the evenness of mind, the tranquility of mind, and the neutrality of mind present in the fourth jhāna.
"Mindfulness" refers to that mindfulness, recollection, and so forth, up to right mindfulness, which is directed toward equanimity in the fourth jhāna.

"Purified by equanimity and mindfulness" means that in the fourth jhāna both equanimity and mindfulness are pure, cleansed, thoroughly purified, completely purified, bright, stainless, free from defilements, become supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability— thus it is "purified by equanimity and mindfulness."
"Preceded by reflection on the nature of things" (*dhammatakkapurejava*): "reflection on the nature of things" (*dhammatakka*) refers to right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*).
That is present at the beginning, it is prior, and it is the precursor to the liberation through higher knowledge; thus it is "preceded by reflection on the nature of things.
Alternatively, "reflection on the nature of things" refers to right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*).
"It comes first, it precedes, it is the forerunner of the liberation through final knowledge"—thus too there is the precedence of the investigation of states.
Alternatively, "investigation of states" refers to the insight prior to the four paths.
That [insight] comes first, it precedes, it is the forerunner of the liberation through final knowledge.
"Thus, with the investigation of phenomena as its precursor, I declare the liberation through final knowledge. Here, "liberation through final knowledge" refers to the liberation of arahantship.
"I declare the liberation of arahantship"—that is, I announce it, teach it, describe it, establish it, reveal it, analyze it, clarify it, and make it manifest.
"I declare it to be the liberation through final knowledge;
it is the breaking up of ignorance.
Here, "ignorance" (avijjā) means lack of knowledge regarding suffering... [and so on] ...ignorance is delusion, the root of unwholesomeness.
"Breaking up" means the breaking up, abandoning, subsiding, relinquishing, and calming of ignorance, which is the deathless Nibbāna—
this is the breaking up of ignorance.
Thus the Blessed One said:
“Purified by equanimity and mindfulness,
preceded by reflection on the Dhamma—
this I call the liberation through final knowledge.”
And the breaking up of ignorance.
What is the fetter of the world?
And what is its investigation?
By the abandoning of what is Nibbāna said to be attained?
What is the fetter of the world? [The answer is: The fetter, the attachment, the bond, the defilement of the world.
“By what is the world bound, engaged, occupied, and thoroughly attached; by what is it clung to, fastened, and obstructed?”—What is the fetter of the world?
What is its investigation? What is its wandering, its investigation, and its thorough investigation?
"By what does the world move, roam about, and wander?
What is its deliberation?
By the abandoning of what is it called 'Nibbāna'? [The answer is: "By the abandoning, the subsiding, and the relinquishing of what..."
"Nibbāna is said, proclaimed, spoken of, uttered, illuminated, and designated as 'the subsiding'—
by the abandoning of what is it called 'Nibbāna'? It was for this reason that the brahmin spoke thus.
“What is the fetter of the world?
What is its deliberation? By the abandoning of what is one released from suffering?”
“Nibbāna,” it is said.
The world is bound by the fetter of delight;
it is the pondering of thought.
Through the complete abandoning of craving, it is called "Nibbāna.
The world is bound by delight; thus, "delight" is said to be craving.
Whatever lust, infatuation, ... [as above] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness—this is called delight (*nandī*).

Whatever delight there is in the world that is a fetter, a snag, a bond, an affliction—it is through this delight that the world is joined, yoked, bound, and fully attached; it is snagged, ensnared, and obstructed.
Thus, "the world has the fetter of delight."
"Discerning of thought.
As for "thoughts," there are nine thoughts:
sensual thought, ill-will thought, cruelty thought, thought of relatives, thought of country, thought of immortality, [thought of gain, thought of fame, and thought of praise].
Thought associated with the desire to harm others, thought associated with gain, honor, and fame, and thought associated with not being treated with contempt—
these are called the nine thoughts.
These nine thoughts are the wandering, the deliberating, and the scrutinizing of the world.
"The world moves, wanders, and roams about by means of these nine types of thought;
this is the investigation of thought.
Through the complete abandoning of craving, it is called Nibbāna."
"Craving" means craving for forms … [and so on] … craving for mental phenomena (*dhamma*).

"Nibbāna is said to be through the complete abandoning of craving": through the complete abandoning, the subsiding, the relinquishing, and the allaying of craving, it is called Nibbāna; it is spoken of, declared, stated, uttered, illustrated, and designated as "Nibbāna"—thus, "Nibbāna is said to be through the complete abandoning of craving."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"The world is bound by delight;
it is the pondering of thought."
“By the complete abandoning of craving,
it is called Nibbāna.
How does one who is mindful while walking...
Consciousness ceases;
we wish to hear from you the words regarding that which he came to ask the Blessed One.
"How does one who walks mindfully? means: how does one who walks, dwells, moves about, conducts himself, protects himself, maintains himself, and sustains himself while being mindful?
"How does consciousness cease for one who walks mindfully? means: consciousness ceases, subsides, comes to an end, and becomes stilled.
“Consciousness ceases.

“We have come to question the Blessed One”: we have come, approached, arrived, reached, and met together with the Buddha, the Blessed One, in order to question him, to ask him, to entreat him, to request him, and to please him—thus, “we have come to question the Blessed One.”
“We hear that word of yours”:
“That” means we hear, learn, memorize, retain, and discern your word—your speech, your teaching, your instruction, and what has been taught.
Thus: “We hear that word of yours.”
Therefore that brahmin said:
“How does consciousness cease for one who lives in being? How does one become cool and attain Nibbāna?”
"He has come to question the Blessed One;
let us hear your words on this. [The Blessed One said:
"Both internally and externally..."
For one who does not delight in feeling,
for the mindful one who lives thus,
consciousness ceases.
"Not delighting in feeling internally and externally" means that while dwelling contemplating feelings in feelings internally,
one does not delight in feeling, does not welcome it, and does not cling to it;
one abandons, dispels, brings to an end, and causes the disappearance of delighting, welcoming, clinging, grasping, misapprehension, and insistence.
Dwelling contemplating feelings in external feelings, he does not delight in feeling, does not welcome it,

and does not remain attached to it; he abandons, dispels, eliminates, and brings to non-existence the delighting, welcoming, and attachment, as well as the grasping, the misapprehension, and the dogmatic insistence.
Dwelling contemplating feelings in feelings internally and externally, he does not delight in feeling, does not welcome it,
and does not remain attached to it; he abandons, dispels, brings to an end, and causes the disappearance of delighting, welcoming, attachment, grasping, misapprehension, and insistence.
Dwelling contemplating the nature of arising within feelings, he does not delight in feeling,

does not welcome it, and does not cling to it. He abandons, dispels, brings to an end, and causes the disappearance of delighting, welcoming, and clinging, as well as grasping, misapprehension, and dogmatic adherence.
Dwelling contemplating the nature of vanishing within feelings, he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings; ...pe...
dwelling contemplating the nature of arising and vanishing within feelings, he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings; ...pe...
dwelling contemplating the nature of arising externally in feelings, he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, and he does not delight in feeling.

He does not greet it, nor does he cling to it; he abandons, dispels, brings to an end, and causes the disappearance of delighting, greeting, clinging, grasping, misapprehension, and adherence. Dwelling thus contemplating the nature of vanishing in external feelings, he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... (as above) ...he causes the disappearance of delighting, greeting, clinging, grasping, misapprehension, and adherence. Dwelling thus contemplating the nature of vanishing in internal feelings, he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... (as above) ...he causes the disappearance of delighting, greeting, clinging, grasping, misapprehension, and adherence. Dwelling thus contemplating the nature of vanishing in both internal and external feelings, he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... (as above) ...he causes the disappearance of delighting, greeting, clinging, grasping, misapprehension, and adherence. Dwelling thus contemplating the nature of vanishing in feelings as they arise, he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... (as above) ...he causes the disappearance of delighting, greeting, clinging, grasping, misapprehension, and adherence. Dwelling thus contemplating the nature of vanishing in feelings as they persist, he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... (as above) ...he causes the disappearance of delighting, greeting, clinging, grasping, misapprehension, and adherence. Dwelling thus contemplating the nature of vanishing in feelings as they pass away, he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... (as above) ...he causes the disappearance of delighting, greeting, clinging, grasping, misapprehension, and adherence. Dwelling thus contemplating the nature of vanishing in feelings as they arise, persist, and pass away, he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... (as above) ...he causes the disappearance of delighting, greeting, clinging, grasping, misapprehension, and adherence. Dwelling thus contemplating the nature of vanishing in the body, he dwells contemplating the body in the body... (as above) ...he causes the disappearance of delighting, greeting, clinging, grasping, misapprehension, and adherence. Dwelling thus contemplating the nature of vanishing in the mind, he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind... (as above) ...he causes the disappearance of delighting, greeting, clinging, grasping, misapprehension, and adherence. Dwelling thus contemplating the nature of vanishing in phenomena, he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena... (as above) ...he causes the disappearance of delighting, greeting, clinging, grasping, misapprehension, and adherence. Dwelling thus contemplating the nature of vanishing in phenomena as they arise, he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena... (as above) ...he causes the disappearance of delighting, greeting, clinging, grasping, misapprehension, and adherence. Dwelling thus contemplating the nature of vanishing in phenomena as they persist, he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena... (as above) ...he causes the disappearance of delighting, greeting, clinging, grasping, misapprehension, and adherence. Dwelling thus contemplating the nature of vanishing in phenomena as they pass away, he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena... (as above) ...he causes the disappearance of delighting, greeting, clinging, grasping, misapprehension, and adherence. Dwelling thus contemplating the nature of vanishing in phenomena as they arise, persist, and pass away, he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena... (as above) ...he causes the disappearance of delighting, greeting, clinging, grasping, misapprehension, and adherence. Dwelling thus with mindfulness and clear comprehension, he overcomes fear and dread. He does not become excited or agitated by sounds that have arisen from outside. Even if a violent band of thieves were to attack him, or even if a violent storm of wind and rain were to strike him, he would not be overcome by fear or terror. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, this is the domain of the Tathāgata, his sphere of mastery, and it is here that the Tathāgata attains supreme self-mastery. It is for this reason, Ānanda, that a bhikkhu who is a trainee, desiring to attain the unsurpassed security from bondage, should dwell contemplating the nature of vanishing in feelings, whether internal or external, or both internal and external, or as they arise, persist, and pass away. This is called the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. And what, Ānanda, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? It is the complete fading away and cessation of that very craving—freedom from desire, relinquishment, letting go, and non-attachment. This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. And what, Ānanda, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is called the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Now, Ānanda, when a noble disciple has thus understood these four noble truths as they really are, with their aspects and their particulars, then, Ānanda, this noble disciple is called one who has entered the stream, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of attaining enlightenment.

Furthermore, Ānanda, when a noble disciple has thus understood these four noble truths as they really are, with their aspects and their particulars, then, Ānanda, this noble disciple is called one who has attained the fruit of once-returning; having returned to this world only once more, he will make an end of suffering. Furthermore, Ānanda, when a noble disciple has thus understood these four noble truths as they really are, with their aspects and their particulars, then, Ānanda, this noble disciple is called one who has attained the fruit of non-returning; having passed away from this world, he will be reborn in the higher realms and will there attain final Nibbāna without ever returning from that world. Furthermore, Ānanda, when a noble disciple has thus understood these four noble truths as they really are, with their aspects and their particulars, then, Ānanda, this noble disciple is called one who has attained the fruit of Arahantship; he is a destroyer of the taints, one who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, achieved his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge."
Dwelling contemplating the nature of arising in feelings externally, he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings; ... pe ...
dwelling contemplating the nature of arising internally and externally in feelings, he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings; ... pe ...
dwelling contemplating the nature of vanishing internally and externally in feelings, he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings; ... pe ...
Dwelling contemplating the nature of arising and passing away internally and externally, he dwells contemplating feelings as feelings;
he does not delight in feeling, does not welcome it, and does not become attached to it.
He abandons, dispels, brings to an end, and causes the disappearance of delighting, welcoming, attachment, grasping, misapprehension, and insistence.
Dwelling thus contemplating feelings in feelings by way of these twelve aspects … [as before] … he brings them to non-existence.
Alternatively, seeing feeling as impermanent, he does not delight in feeling, does not welcome it, and does not cling to it.
He abandons, dispels, brings to an end, and causes the disappearance of delighting in, welcoming, cleaving to, grasping, misapprehending, and adhering [to it].
He regards feeling as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as a calamity, and as an affliction... [and so forth]...

Seeing [feeling] as an escape, one does not delight in feeling, does not welcome it, and does not cling to it; one abandons, dispels, brings to an end, and eliminates the delighting, welcoming, clinging, grasping, misapprehension, and adherence [toward it].
Dwelling thus contemplating feelings in feelings through these forty modes, one does not delight in feeling, does not welcome it, and does not cling to it;
one abandons the delighting, welcoming, clinging, grasping, misapprehension, and adherence [toward it].
"He dispels it, brings it to an end, and leads it to non-existence" means:
for one who does not delight in feeling internally or externally.
"Thus living with mindfulness" means: thus living, dwelling, moving, acting, maintaining, preserving, sustaining, and supporting oneself while being mindful and clearly comprehending.
"For one who lives thus,
consciousness ceases": the consciousness associated with the formation of merit, the consciousness associated with the formation of demerit,
and the consciousness associated with the formation of the imperturbable cease, subside, come to an end, and become stilled.
consciousness ceases.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Internally and externally..."
For one who does not delight in feeling,
for one who lives thus with mindfulness,
consciousness comes to cease.
With the conclusion of the verse... [as before] ...
"The Blessed One is my teacher, venerable sir; I am his disciple.
This is the thirteenth exposition: The Question of the Young Brahmin Udaya.
